critical_caution: This is one of Dick's most directly autobiographical pieces of published fiction, written in March 1975 in the immediate aftermath of the '2-3-74' visionary experiences he spent the rest of his life trying to interpret in the Exegesis. The narrator explicitly becomes 'Philip,' recounting real childhood details (Berkeley, Hillside Grammar School, a grandmother, a girlfriend named Ysabel Lomax, a therapist) alongside the fictional frame-narrative of a Roman priest. Read this dossier's synopsis as describing a first-person account Dick offered of his own anamnesis experience in fictionalized form, not as ordinary invented plot.

work.title: The Eye of the Sibyl
work.first_publication: The Dark Side, edited by Damon Knight, 1976

source.note: Locator into the git-ignored reading corpus. No primary text is stored here.

reading.synopsis: An aging Roman priest named Philos Diktos of Tyana ('Philip' transliterated into Greek and Latin) confesses, near the end of his life, a secret witnessed decades earlier at the temple of the Cumaean Sibyl, shortly after the assassination of Julius Caesar. Arriving at the temple before dawn, he sees the Sibyl in conference with two 'Immortals' — alien or divine beings communicating via a telephone-like device — who tell her that Rome will survive under Augustus but that two thousand years of darkness will follow a coming failed religious mission (a 'Light Creature' who will be tortured and murdered like Caesar), after which civilization will begin to question its true origins again. The Sibyl then places a third eye — the 'Eye of the Sibyl,' also called the Gorgon's Eye — on her forehead to see further down the corridors of time, and the shock of what she sees causes her to collapse; in the moment of contact, the narrator himself is pulled forward through those same corridors and becomes, without transition, a boy named Philip growing up in twentieth-century Berkeley — recognizable in every biographical detail as Dick's own childhood, adolescence, and early ambition to write science fiction. As adult Philip, in 1974, sudden phosphene visions and a jolt of anamnesis restore his memory of having been the Roman priest, and the same two Immortals reappear to tell him that with no Sibyl left to advise the Republic, they now work directly through ordinary people's dreams to wake them from the tyranny they live under. The story closes with the aged Roman narrator quoting Virgil's Fourth Eclogue — itself long read as an eerie premonition of Christian nativity — as a coded prophecy that the two-thousand-year winter will end, addressed as much to Dick's own 1970s American readers as to his fictional Roman audience.

structure.form: short story in three movements: the Roman frame, the transposition into Dick's own childhood and adolescence, the return and the prophecy
movements: Philos Diktos witnesses the Sibyl consulting the Immortals about Rome's future and a coming two-thousand-year dark age, then sees her Third Eye and its prophecy overwhelm her.
Without any narrative seam, the story becomes an autobiographical account of Philip's Berkeley childhood, adolescent ambitions, and recurring dreams of Rome, snakes, and alien contact.

In 1974, anamnesis restores the Roman memory; the Immortals explain they now act through dreams alone, and the aged Roman narrator closes with Virgil's Fourth Eclogue as prophecy of the coming end of the dark age.
structure.point_of_view: first person throughout, but the identity of the 'I' shifts without acknowledgment from the Roman priest to the Berkeley child to the adult writer — the collapse of narrative distance between these is the story's entire argument, not a technical lapse.
structure.central_device: A single continuous consciousness experienced across two thousand years and two identities, presented not as reincarnation-as-plot-device but as the literal claim underlying Dick's own 2-3-74 experience of anamnesis.

characters.name: Philos Diktos of Tyana / Philip
characters.role: narrator, both Roman priest and twentieth-century science fiction writer
characters.note: The Greek/Latin name is a direct transliteration of 'Philip Dick' — the story's clearest signal that the frame narrative and the autobiography are the same claim made twice.

characters.name: The Sibyl
characters.note: Consults alien 'Immortals' via a technological rather than mystical interface, and possesses a third Eye that lets her see forward in time at a cost of real physical and psychological shock.

characters.name: The Immortals (J'Annis, F'fr'am)
characters.note: Present in Roman antiquity and again in 1974, explaining that without a Sibyl to consult directly, they now work through ordinary people's dreams — Dick's own explanation, transposed into the fiction, for what he believed was happening to him.

characters.name: Ysabel Lomax
characters.note: Present as the adult Philip's skeptical, status-conscious girlfriend in 1974, and reappears in the Roman frame's climactic vision with a third eye of her own — the story's two timelines visibly bleeding into each other through her.

settings.name: The temple at Cumae
settings.note: Where the Sibylline oracle operates through what the narrator describes in explicitly technological terms — a gas-filled chamber, a telephone-like device, alien visitors in transparent capsules.

settings.name: Berkeley, California, mid-twentieth century
settings.note: Rendered in specific, verifiable autobiographical detail — Hillside Grammar School, the Berkeley Daily Gazette, a grandmother's disapproval of comics — presented with the same narrative authority as the Roman frame.

motifs: A third eye as the physical organ of prophetic or trans-temporal sight, appearing on the Sibyl, on Ysabel in a vision, and implicitly on the narrator himself through anamnesis
Snakes as recurring dream-wisdom imagery, tied explicitly to the caduceus and to ancient oracle traditions
A two-thousand-year dark age framed as literal historical prophecy rather than metaphor, bridging Roman antiquity and 1970s America
Alien/divine 'Immortals' who once advised rulers directly and now work covertly through dreams
Virgil's Fourth Eclogue quoted as a real historical text whose messianic ambiguity is claimed, within the story, to be genuine prophecy rather than later Christian misreading
reading.significance: Dick's own letters date this story with unusual precision — written in a single morning in March 1975, mailed to editors Art and Michele with visible anxiety about its reception, and connected explicitly to a recent public speech: 'between my speech and this story... I've blown my cover... I'm amazed that I felt, from the start, that I should keep absolutely quiet about it.' That 'it' is the 2-3-74 experience itself, and this story is one of Dick's earliest attempts to disclose it publicly in any form, fictional or otherwise — predating most of the Exegesis by which he would spend the rest of his life trying to work out what had happened to him. Sutin notes the piece was submitted for a comic-book/movie collaboration and judged 'too intricate' for that medium, which is itself telling: the story resists being read as a plotted narrative because it is not primarily plot but testimony.
reading.closing_note: The aged Roman narrator addresses his closing prophecy explicitly past his own Roman audience, to 'far along the corridors of time, in the United States' — a direct authorial address breaking the fiction's own frame to speak to Dick's actual 1970s readers.

distinctive_terms.label: Apollo
distinctive_terms.note: Named directly in the closing Virgil quotation as 'the rightful king... restored.'

distinctive_terms.label: Anamnesis
distinctive_terms.note: Dick's own technical term (from Platonic philosophy, meaning the recollection of the soul's prior knowledge) for the narrator's sudden restoration of his Roman memory — used here in fiction exactly as he uses it throughout the Exegesis.

distinctive_terms.label: Iron
distinctive_terms.note: The 'Iron Prison' whose fall the closing prophecy announces — one of Dick's own recurring names, elsewhere in the Exegesis, for the world's fallen condition.

thematic_links_proposed.basis: a direct fictionalized account of anamnesis, alien/divine advisory beings, and a two-thousand-year dark age framed as literal religious history
a single continuous consciousness split across two thousand years and two names, restored to itself through a sudden recovered memory
the entire narrative device depends on genuine, non-metaphorical travel and contact across two millennia

pkd_on_this_work.summary: Exceptionally well-documented in Dick's own letters: composition date, submission anxiety, and — most significantly — his own statement that this story, alongside a recent public speech, publicly disclosed the experience he had otherwise resolved to keep silent about.

evidence.quote: Here is a 14-page piece (about 3,000 words) for you called "The Eye of the Sibyl." It is I think a story which you can illustrate in a vivid and compelling way.
evidence.reading: Dated March 30, 1975 in the letters — establishing precise composition timing, just over a year after the 2-3-74 experiences began.

evidence.quote: I guess between my speech and this story, "The Eye of the Sibyl," I've blown my cover. I'm amazed that I felt, from the start, that I should keep absolutely quiet about it;
evidence.reading: The single most important piece of evidence in this dossier: Dick's own acknowledgment that this story was a deliberate, anxious act of public disclosure of the anamnesis experience, alongside a public speech from the same period.

evidence.quote: It only took me half a morning to write the dam thing; for your records it's a story called "The Eye of the Sibyl."
evidence.reading: Confirms the story was written quickly, in one sitting — consistent with its reading as urgent testimony rather than a carefully plotted commercial piece.

evidence.author: Lawrence Sutin
evidence.quote: Phil now proposed a collaboration; but the story Phil submitted in March 1975 -- "The Eye of the Sibyl" -- was, like the 1974 Ubik screenplay, too intricate for adaptation to the intended (comic book/movie) medium.
evidence.reading: Confirms the composition date and the story's original intended market (a visual adaptation project), and that its density made it unsuitable — a reasonable outcome for a piece built as testimony rather than plot.

open_questions: This story predates most of the Exegesis's developed vocabulary (the Empire never ended, VALIS, the Black Iron Prison as a fully worked concept) but already uses 'anamnesis' and 'Iron Prison' — worth tracing how much of Dick's later theological vocabulary was already present this early, in March 1975.

The 'speech' Dick references in the same breath as this story — is that the Vancouver 'If You Find This World Bad, You Should See Some of the Others' address, or the earlier Metz speech? Dating this precisely would sharpen the disclosure timeline.

Ysabel Lomax appears with a third eye in the Roman-timeline vision but is Philip's mundane, skeptical girlfriend in the Berkeley timeline — is this detail addressed anywhere in Dick's own commentary, or is it left for the reader to notice unassisted?
